summary:
Artvin stands under the national framework of Turkey, where hostility toward trans people has been organised into documented state policy rather than left as residual prejudice. Kaos GL's LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025, launched under the title "A major siege against LGBTI+ people in 2025: Hostility turned into state policy", recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, alongside 299 detention decisions — 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record — and systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people. The launch presentation by lawyer Kerem Dikmen set out how senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions under a "Year of the Family" banner created a climate that encouraged violations, with regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricting freedom of expression and artistic freedom.

A draft omnibus law, the 11th Judicial Package, was reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025. It would amend the Turkish penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality", criminalise taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with penalties of up to four years in prison, raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care including surgery from 18 to 25 with a requirement of permanent infertility, and punish health professionals who perform such care. Human Rights Watch calls it one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades; 15 Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose the draft. The measure had not been passed when reported, but its pending status has not prevented authorities from acting as though the prohibitions were already in force.

The Erdoğan government has repeatedly framed its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals", language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people. Street-level enforcement illustrates the gap between the draft's status and its application: in 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release, with legal experts arguing that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that no fines were issued but that the police documented them anyway, and that enforcement was already being applied to her before any new law had passed.

Foreign visitors face a direct outing risk at these interactions. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Any checkpoint stop is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Prison conditions form part of the same regime. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025, and the case confirmed that Turkey places trans prisoners according to their registered sex, a trans man having been held in a women's prison. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation, reporting that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case was raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, placing custody conditions for trans prisoners under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies.
tangentialFactors:
The pattern documented for Turkey is longstanding rather than newly minted. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. That report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the regime's depth, not as a statement of current law.

Enforcement examples in the inventory come from Istanbul rather than from Artvin, and the province of Artvin has no trans-specific incident recorded in the sources supplied. The national figures — 313 violations, 299 detention decisions, six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025 — describe the country as a whole, and a visitor to Artvin should read them as the baseline rather than assume that a quieter province is a safer one. Border and transit provinces in eastern Turkey sit under the same national police commands, the same identification-check practice and the same penal code as the metropolitan districts where the documented stops occurred.

The draft package's provisions on health care and on ceremony participation would, if enacted, change the legal position of any trans or same-sex couple travelling together, since participation in an engagement or marriage ceremony is itself proposed as an offence. Opposition to the draft from 15 LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association indicates organised domestic resistance, but neither that opposition nor the pending status of the bill has thus far altered enforcement practice on the ground.
localsOnly:
Residents of Artvin live under the same national administrative and prosecutorial machinery as the rest of Turkey, and the restrictions documented in 2025 bear directly on daily life rather than only on visitors. Kaos GL's reporting describes instructions issued to public institutions under a "Year of the Family" banner and regulatory bodies restricting freedom of expression and artistic freedom, which constrains what LGBT residents can publish, perform and organise.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Access to transition-related care for residents narrowed in 2025. The Health Ministry regulation, following the Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option on medical-board reports and required e-reports to be issued, which channels trans patients into official records flagged for gender reassignment and risks both profiling and restricted access. The draft 11th Judicial Package would go further, raising the age threshold for gender-affirming care to 25 and conditioning it on permanent infertility while punishing the clinicians who provide it.

Document markers are a resident problem as much as a visitor one. Placement of trans prisoners by registered sex, the psychiatric evaluation of four transgender inmates shortly before the Sincan death, and the requirement that medical boards record gender reassignment as an official reason all indicate that the state's records of a person's sex are treated as authoritative against their presentation.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents a trans-specific incident, police practice, healthcare restriction or facility in Artvin province itself. The province-level record is therefore an application of the national framework, not an independent finding, and any Artvin-specific enforcement pattern remains unresolved on the material supplied.

The 11th Judicial Package was reported as a draft on 29 October 2025 and had not been passed at that point. Whether it has since been enacted, amended or withdrawn is not sourced here, and the same applies to the precise legal force of the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation outside the reporting cited.

Whether a trans visitor can change a gender marker on a Turkish visa, residence permit or on their own foreign passport for entry purposes is not addressed by any source in the inventory. The identification-check risk described rests on the general requirement to carry original photo ID and on documented GBT stops in Istanbul; no source establishes how often such stops occur in Artvin or what follows from a marker mismatch.

The Human Rights Watch 2008 report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is included only as historical evidence of the regime's depth. It should not be read as a statement of current Turkish law.
